content: The health care industry, also referred to as the health profession, is a sector that involves the application of specialized skills, judgment, and services aimed at maintaining or improving the health of individuals. It also encompasses the treatment and care of individuals who are injured, ill, disabled, or otherwise infirm. The delivery of modern health care relies on a growing network of trained professionals who collaborate as part of an interdisciplinary team. The health care industry is one of the largest and fastest-growing sectors globally. In many developed nations, it accounts for more than 10% of the gross domestic product (GDP), making it a significant component of national economies. For example, in 2003, health care expenditures in the United States consumed 15.3% of the country's GDP, the highest proportion among all nations. By 2006, U.S. health care expenditures reached $2.2 trillion, and in 2007, an estimated $7,498 was spent per person on health care. Projections indicated that by 2016, this figure would rise to $12,782 per person, with health care costs accounting for 19.6% of the U.S. GDP. Comparatively, in 2001, the average health care expenditure among OECD countries was 8.4% of GDP, with the United States (13.9%), Switzerland (10.9%), and Germany (10.7%) leading in spending. A health care provider or professional is an individual or organization that delivers health care services in a systematic and professional manner to those in need. The delivery of health care services typically involves payment, either directly from the patient or through the patient’s insurance provider. In some cases, services may be funded by government programs, such as the National Health Service (NHS) in the United Kingdom, or provided by charitable organizations or volunteers, particularly in low-income regions. Health care services are delivered in various ways. The most common method is face-to-face interaction, where the health care provider and the patient meet in person. This is the standard approach in general medical practice in most countries. However, with advancements in telecommunications technology, remote health care delivery is becoming increasingly prevalent. This form of care, known as in absentia health care, involves communication between the provider and the patient through methods such as phone calls, video conferencing, emails, text messages, or other digital platforms, eliminating the need for physical presence.
